anchorData: CLASS: Grade 10 Green, Lakeview Senior School, Kisumu. 40 learners, each gave ONE main way of travelling to school. RAW LIST in learner order 1-40 (W=walk, M=matatu, B=boda boda, Bi=bicycle, C=private car, S=school bus): 1 W, 2 M, 3 W, 4 S, 5 M, 6 W, 7 B, 8 W, 9 M, 10 C, 11 W, 12 M, 13 Bi, 14 W, 15 M, 16 W, 17 S, 18 M, 19 W, 20 B, 21 M, 22 W, 23 C, 24 W, 25 M, 26 S, 27 W, 28 Bi, 29 M, 30 W, 31 B, 32 M, 33 W, 34 C, 35 S, 36 M, 37 W, 38 Bi, 39 B, 40 M. FREQUENCY TABLE (total 40): Walk 14; Matatu 12; Boda boda 4; Bicycle 3; Private car 3; School bus 4. PERCENTAGES: Walk 35%, Matatu 30%, Boda boda 10%, Bicycle 7.5%, Private car 7.5%, School bus 10% (sum 100%). Walk + matatu = 26 learners = 65%. PIE CHART: 360 / 40 = 9 degrees per learner. Walk 126, Matatu 108, Boda boda 36, Bicycle 27, Private car 27, School bus 36 (sum 360). The mode of travel is Walk (14). Mean and median do not apply to travel mode because it is categories, not numbers. BAR GRAPH: scale 0 to 14 or 16 on the frequency axis, steps of 2. MISLEADING GRAPH EXAMPLE: if the vertical axis starts at 2 instead of 0, the walk bar is 12 units tall and the bicycle bar is 1 unit tall, so walking looks 12 times bicycle when the true ratio is 14:3, about 4.7 times. OTHER COMPLETE SETS. (a) Number of siblings, same 40 learners: 0 siblings 5 learners; 1 sibling 9; 2 siblings 12; 3 siblings 8; 4 siblings 4; 5 siblings 2 (total 40). Sum of f x = 0+9+24+24+16+10 = 83. Mean = 83/40 = 2.075, about 2.1. Mode = 2. Median = the average of the 20th and 21st values. Cumulative frequencies are 5, 14, 26, so both are 2 and the median is 2. (b) 800 m training times in seconds for 7 runners in an Eldoret club group (ordered): 104, 105, 105, 106, 107, 108, 130 (the 130 runner had a cold). Sum = 765. Mean = 765/7 = 109.3 s to 1 d.p. Median = 4th value = 106 s. Mode = 105 s. Without the 130 s time, the other six have mean 105.8 s (635/6 = 105.83). (c) Daily mandazi sales by Mama Achieng at Kisumu Kibuye market: Mon 40, Tue 45, Wed 42, Thu 50, Fri 65, Sat 30, Sun 20. Total = 292. Highest is Friday (65), lowest is Sunday (20). (d) Trees in the school compound (30 trees): Grevillea 12, Cypress 8, Eucalyptus 6, Neem 4 (total 30). (e) Monthly budget of the Wanjiru family in Nairobi, KSh 30,000: Food 12,000 (40%, 144 degrees); Rent 7,500 (25%, 90 degrees); School fees 4,500 (15%, 54 degrees); Transport 3,000 (10%, 36 degrees); Savings 3,000 (10%, 36 degrees). Angles sum to 360.
characters: Mr Otieno: the principal of Lakeview Senior School, Kisumu. He must choose between a school bus route, a bicycle shed and a second lunch serving, and he has money for only one. Mr Kamau: the Grade 10 Green Essential Mathematics teacher who sets up the data collection. Grade 10 Green: 40 learners, the data source for all travel data. Three conflicting voices are quoted in Lesson 1: Atieno says 'Almost everyone walks'; Brian says 'Most of us come by matatu'; Zawadi says 'The bus is always full'. Zawadi's remark is about the school's single 14-seater bus serving the whole school, so the class count (4 on the bus) cannot confirm or refute it. Mama Achieng: sells mandazi at Kibuye market, Kisumu (daily sales data). Eldoret club group: 7 runners in an anonymous Eldoret training group (fictional; no real athletes are named in the data). Wanjiru family: a Nairobi family with a monthly budget of KSh 30,000. Lakeview compound: has 30 trees (tree data). All learner names are fictional. Class data covers only Grade 10 Green, not the whole school.
outcome: The raw list of 40 responses cannot settle the argument, but the frequency table, bar graph and pie chart show that walking is the largest group (14 of 40, 35%) and matatu is second (12 of 40, 30%). So 'almost everyone walks' and 'most come by matatu' are both wrong, since neither is more than half, although together they account for 65%. Only 3 of 40 (7.5%) cycle and 4 of 40 (10%) use the school bus, so this class gives little support for a bicycle shed. Learners advise Mr Otieno to put no money into a shed on this evidence, and to collect the same data from the whole school before deciding on the bus or lunch serving, because one class is a small sample. Mean, median and mode agree for siblings (about 2) but differ for the runner times (mean 109.3, median 106, mode 105) because one slow time pulls the mean up, so the best summary and graph depend on the type of data and the question.
conventions: Terms: raw data = unorganised list; frequency (f) = number of times a value occurs; tally marks grouped in fives (four strokes crossed by a fifth); frequency table has columns Value (or Category), Tally, Frequency. Categorical data = names/categories (travel mode, tree type); discrete numerical data = counted numbers (siblings, mandazi sold). Only UNGROUPED data is used; there are no class intervals. Total frequency is written n or Σf. Mean = Σfx ÷ Σf (the sum of every value divided by how many values there are), written as 'mean', never 'average'. Mode = most frequent value or category. Median = middle value of the ordered data: for odd n it is the ((n+1)/2)th value; for even n it is the mean of the two middle values. Round to 1 decimal place and give units (seconds, KSh, learners). Percentage = f / n x 100. Pie angle = f / n x 360 degrees, drawn with a protractor, angles must sum to 360. Bar graphs: bars of equal width with gaps, for categories, frequency axis starts at 0, both axes labelled, with a title. Line graphs: points joined by straight lines, for change over time, time on the horizontal axis. Currency is KSh. Anchor numbers are always quoted exactly as in anchorData. Travel groups are always named Walk, Matatu, Boda boda, Bicycle, Private car, School bus, in that order. Digital tools means a spreadsheet or graphing app on a phone, tablet or computer (offline-capable).

lessonMap.focus: Whose claim is right? Launching the principal's problem
lessonMap.teaches: Raw data is hard to use as evidence: learners predict the travel split, collect the 40 responses and see that the unorganised list does not settle the claims; the DQB and first draft model are started
lessonMap.buildsOn: No earlier lesson; builds on prior Grade 9 knowledge of collecting data
lessonMap.usesData: Full raw list of 40 travel responses and the three claims by Atieno, Brian and Zawadi. The totals are NOT revealed yet.

lessonMap.teaches: Organising raw data into a tally and frequency table for categorical and discrete data, and checking that the frequencies add to the total
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 1: the raw list of 40 responses and the unsettled claims
lessonMap.usesData: Travel frequency table (14, 12, 4, 3, 3, 4 = 40) with percentages; tree data (12, 8, 6, 4 = 30) as practice

lessonMap.teaches: Finding the mode from a frequency table and calculating the mean using Σfx ÷ Σf for ungrouped data
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 2: building and reading frequency tables, including the f column
lessonMap.usesData: Siblings table (mean 83/40 = 2.1, mode 2); mode of travel = Walk

lessonMap.focus: Median and choosing the best measure
lessonMap.teaches: Finding the median from ordered data (odd and even n) and deciding whether mean, median or mode best represents the data, including the effect of an outlier
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 3: mode and mean calculations; Lesson 2: ordered frequency lists and cumulative counting
lessonMap.usesData: Siblings median 2 (20th and 21st values); runner times (mean 109.3, median 106, mode 105, mean 105.8 without 130)

lessonMap.teaches: Drawing bar graphs for categories and line graphs for change over time, and choosing which graph suits which type of data
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 2: frequency tables as the source for graph data; Lesson 4: the idea that a representation should match the data
lessonMap.usesData: Travel frequency table for the bar graph; mandazi sales Mon to Sun for the line graph

lessonMap.teaches: Converting frequencies to angles (f / n x 360) and drawing and labelling a pie chart; comparing a pie chart with a bar graph for the same data
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 2: percentages and totals; Lesson 5: the bar graph of the same travel data
lessonMap.usesData: Travel angles (126, 108, 36, 27, 27, 36 = 360); Wanjiru family budget angles (144, 90, 54, 36, 36 = 360)

lessonMap.focus: Reading graphs critically and using digital tools
lessonMap.teaches: Interpreting graphs and charts to draw and defend conclusions, spotting misleading graphs (truncated axis) and recreating graphs with a spreadsheet or app
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 5 and 6: bar, line and pie graphs; Lesson 4: choosing measures
lessonMap.usesData: Misleading bar graph with axis starting at 2 (walk 12 units vs bicycle 1 unit, true ratio 14:3); mandazi line graph; travel pie chart and bar graph

lessonMap.teaches: Synthesising the whole statistics cycle (collect, organise, summarise, display, interpret) into a data-based recommendation and answering the driving question; no new technique
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 1 to 7: raw data, frequency tables, mean/median/mode, graphs, pie charts, critical reading
lessonMap.usesData: All travel data (35% walk, 30% matatu, 65% together, bus 10%, bicycle 7.5%) and the recommendation in the outcome: no shed on this evidence, collect whole-school data before deciding on bus or lunch
